# Baseline


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

The baseline scores small models before any fine-tuning, on the frozen
test set and with the code checks, so that fine-tuning has a fair number
to beat. Untuned models get a short prompt: the teacher’s context and
rules, and two worked examples. The teacher’s bad message and
failure-mode list would likely confuse a model of 1 to 2B parameters.
The fine-tuned models get a one-line instruction instead, which training
needs and the board favours, as [Fine-tuning](06_finetune.ipynb)
explains.

## The student prompt

A first baseline gave one example, with only the 🚨 and ⚠️ markers, and
both models almost never used 👀, although most test items are early:
small models copy the example’s markers over the rules. The two examples
here use all three markers, both kinds of problem, and both values of
`soil_water`:

## Running a model

[`run_model`](https://franckalbinet.github.io/edgeslm/baseline.html#run_model)
writes a message for every row with greedy decoding, so that a run is
reproducible, and checks each one:

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<a
href="https://github.com/franckalbinet/edgeslm/blob/main/edgeslm/baseline.py#L42"
target="_blank" style="float:right; font-size:smaller">source</a>

### run_model

``` python
def run_model(
    model_id:str, # Hugging Face id or local path of an MLX model
    rows:list, # Rows with `id`, `tuple` and `record`
    adapter_path:str=None, # LoRA adapters to apply, for a fine-tuned model
    sp:str=None, # System prompt; the student prompt by default
    max_tokens:int=400, # Longest message to generate
)->list: # One row per input, with the message, its checks and the run's settings
```

*Have `model_id` write and check a message for each row*

This cell wrote the baseline runs of Qwen3.5 0.8B and 2B, in full
precision. Both together took about 18 minutes on an Apple M5, and the
cell does not run in tests:

``` python
test = read_jsonl('../data/test-v1.jsonl')
for m, f in [('mlx-community/Qwen3.5-0.8B-bf16', 'qwen3.5-0.8b'), ('mlx-community/Qwen3.5-2B-bf16', 'qwen3.5-2b')]:
    write_jsonl(f'../data/baseline-v2-{f}.jsonl', run_model(m, test))
```

[`markers`](https://franckalbinet.github.io/edgeslm/baseline.html#markers)
pairs the true severity of each item with the marker the model wrote for
it:

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<a
href="https://github.com/franckalbinet/edgeslm/blob/main/edgeslm/baseline.py#L73"
target="_blank" style="float:right; font-size:smaller">source</a>

### markers

``` python
def markers(
    rows:list, # Scored rows of one run
    test:list, # The test records, which hold each item's true severity
)->collections.Counter:
```

*Count each (true severity, written marker) pair over the items of
`rows`*

The second prompt more than doubled the 0.8B’s score, but neither model
maps the three severities to the three markers. The 0.8B writes 👀 for
nearly every early or moderate item and 🚨 for severe ones. The 2B
writes 🚨 for most items, whatever their severity:

``` python
test = read_jsonl('../data/test-v1.jsonl')
markers(runs['0.8b v2'], test), markers(runs['2b v2'], test)
```

    (Counter({('early', '👀'): 191,
              ('moderate', '👀'): 122,
              ('severe', '🚨'): 103,
              ('moderate', '🚨'): 25,
              ('early', '🚨'): 17,
              ('severe', '👀'): 9,
              ('early', '⚠️'): 1}),
     Counter({('early', '🚨'): 159,
              ('severe', '🚨'): 112,
              ('moderate', '🚨'): 105,
              ('early', '👀'): 34,
              ('moderate', '⚠️'): 27,
              ('early', '⚠️'): 16,
              ('moderate', '👀'): 15}))

The test items are 45% early, so a model that never writes ⚠️ still gets
most markers right, and that is where the 0.8B’s lead over the 2B comes
from:

``` python
Counter(it['severity'] for r in test for it in r['record']['items'])
```

    Counter({'early': 209, 'moderate': 148, 'severe': 112})

The baseline depends heavily on the prompt’s examples. That is itself a
reason to fine-tune: a fine-tuned model should learn the mapping from
many examples, not copy the markers of two.
